nameStory: Field bindweed gets its name from its unstoppable habit of binding itself around other plants as it climbs and spreads through fields and gardens. The word 'bindweed' perfectly captures how this vine wraps around and binds itself to whatever it can grab onto. It's also called 'possession vine' - a name that hints at how completely it can take over a space once it gets established!
description: Field bindweed is a persistent climbing vine that spreads both above and below ground through creeping stems called rhizomes. This herbaceous perennial can stretch its twining stems up to 6 feet long, either crawling along the ground or spiraling up fences, other plants, and any available support. You'll recognize it by its distinctive trumpet-shaped white or pale pink flowers that look like tiny morning glories. Despite its delicate appearance, this European native has become one of the most tenacious weeds across New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small trumpet or funnel-shaped flowers, about 1 inch across, that are white or pale pink with a smooth, papery texture. They have no scent but feel delicate and slightly waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Arrow-shaped leaves with pointed tips and two backward-pointing lobes at the base, alternate along the stem. They feel smooth and slightly thick, with a matte surface that's not shiny.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports, or creeps along the ground in mats. The stems feel smooth and somewhat brittle when fresh.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules that split open when ripe to reveal dark brown seeds. The dried capsules feel papery and rattle when shaken.

habitat: Field bindweed thrives in disturbed soils and sunny locations throughout New England, particularly in agricultural fields, gardens, roadsides, and waste areas. It prefers well-drained soils but is remarkably adaptable to different soil types and conditions. You'll often find it climbing fences, wrapping around crop plants, or forming dense mats in abandoned lots and field edges.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes in late spring, with the distinctive arrow-shaped leaves appearing first. Young stems begin their characteristic counterclockwise twining as they search for support.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from June through August, with the small white or pink trumpet flowers opening in the morning. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and full-sized leaves are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the development of small round seed capsules. Leaves begin to yellow and wither as the plant prepares for dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, but the extensive underground rhizome system remains alive and ready to sprout again in spring. Only dried stems and seed capsules may be visible.

funFact: Field bindweed's underground root system can extend down 20 feet deep and spread outward for 10 feet in all directions - that's why it's nearly impossible to eliminate by pulling and why a single plant can seemingly take over an entire garden bed in just one season!
confusionNotes: Field bindweed is often confused with hedge bindweed (Calystegia species), but field bindweed has much smaller flowers (about 1 inch vs 2-3 inches) and distinctive arrow-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes. Memory trick: 'Field bindweed has petite flowers for the field, hedge bindweed has huge flowers for the hedge.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'morning glory' in some regions, field bindweed is not a true morning glory (Ipomoea species), though they're in the same plant family. True morning glories typically have heart-shaped leaves and larger flowers, while field bindweed has those distinctive arrow-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes.
compareHints: Field bindweed is the most common Convolvulus species in New England, while its relative dwarf morning-glory (Convolvulus tricolor) is mainly found in gardens as an ornamental with distinctive blue, white, and yellow flowers. Field bindweed's flowers are always white or pale pink, never the vibrant blues and yellows of its decorative cousin. Unlike dwarf morning-glory, field bindweed has aggressive underground rhizomes that make it highly invasive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Dwarf morning-glory differs dramatically from its only New England relative, field bindweed, by staying low and bushy rather than climbing, and by having much showier tricolored flowers instead of field bindweed's plain white or pale pink blooms.
